pointers.sentence: `serialize` writes model instances out in a named format, as text in `"json"`, `"jsonl"`, `"xml"` or `"yaml"`, or as lists and dictionaries in the internal `"python"`, and `deserialize` reads the text back as instances not yet saved, each held in a `DeserializedObject` whose save writes the row raw (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py`).

Each format is a module with a `Serializer` and a `Deserializer` class (`django/core/serializers/base.py:Serializer`, `django/core/serializers/base.py:Deserializer`); a built-in one is named by its dotted path in `BUILTIN_SERIALIZERS`.

Each format is a module with a `Serializer` and a `Deserializer` class (`django/core/serializers/base.py:Serializer`, `django/core/serializers/base.py:Deserializer`); a built-in one is named by its dotted path in `BUILTIN_SERIALIZERS`.
The docstring's reason for waiting: a project can set up its settings without minding the order of imports (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py:_load_serializers`).

`register_serializer` imports a format's module; if the import raises `ImportError`, it registers a stand-in whose serializer and deserializer are one `BadSerializer` holding the exception, which raises it when called, so that, the docstring says, the error reaches whoever uses the format (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py:register_serializer`).

`serialize` runs a serializer and returns its `Serializer.getvalue`; `deserialize` returns the deserializer itself, an iterator (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py:serialize`, `django/core/serializers/__init__.py:deserialize`).

`serialize` runs a serializer and returns its `Serializer.getvalue`; `deserialize` returns the deserializer itself, an iterator (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py:serialize`, `django/core/serializers/__init__.py:deserialize`).

`Serializer.serialize` is the same for every format Django ships; a format supplies the hooks it calls as it starts, at the start and the end of each instance, for each field, and as it ends (`django/core/serializers/base.py:Serializer.serialize`).
A field made with `serialize=False` is skipped, and the model's options turn that flag off on the primary key, which is written apart (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.setup_pk`).
A child's parent fields are not local to it: they are the parent's own record (`docs/topics/serialization.txt`).

`Serializer.get_dump_object` makes each from `"model"`, the model's label in lower case, `"pk"`, and `"fields"`, the values by field name (`django/core/serializers/python.py:Serializer.get_dump_object`).

Any other, a string or a UUID among them, is written as what the field's `value_to_string` makes of it, which the field's `to_python` reads back ([A field: the base class](../models/fields.md)) (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.value_to_string`).

A many-to-many field, written only when its through model was made automatically, is the list of the related keys, in the related model's ordering with the key added where that order is not total (`django/core/serializers/python.py:Serializer.handle_m2m_field`).
The documentation's reason is the rows Django makes itself, such as content types, whose keys depend on when they were made (`docs/topics/serialization.txt`).

With `use_natural_foreign_keys=True` a relation to a model with `natural_key` is written as the related object's natural key, and with `use_natural_primary_keys=True` an object with a natural key is written without `"pk"` (`django/core/serializers/python.py:Serializer.handle_fk_field`).
A `natural_key` that returns `()` opts out, and the key is written in its place: with Port's returning `()`, Beagle's home is 1 again (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`).

The JSON serializer writes each object's dictionary as the object ends, passing its remaining options, such as `indent=2`, to the json module's dump (`django/core/serializers/json.py:Serializer.end_object`), with `DjangoJSONEncoder` and `ensure_ascii=False` unless they say otherwise (`django/core/serializers/json.py:Serializer._init_options`).

The JSON serializer writes each object's dictionary as the object ends, passing its remaining options, such as `indent=2`, to the json module's dump (`django/core/serializers/json.py:Serializer.end_object`), with `DjangoJSONEncoder` and `ensure_ascii=False` unless they say otherwise (`django/core/serializers/json.py:Serializer._init_options`).

The encoder writes a datetime in ISO 8601 to the millisecond, or to the second where the milliseconds are zero, with `"Z"` for an offset of zero; a date; a time, refusing one with a zone; a duration in ISO 8601; and a decimal, a UUID or a lazy string as its string (`django/core/serializers/json.py:DjangoJSONEncoder.default`).
Where the milliseconds of a datetime or a time are zero, `DjangoJSONEncoder` wrote `".000"` before (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).

The YAML serializer needs PyYAML, and dumps the whole list at the end with `DjangoSafeDumper`, which writes decimals and times as strings; the comment says a time tagged as Python's could be read in no other language (`django/core/serializers/pyyaml.py:DjangoSafeDumper`).
The XML serializer is built on the base class, and writes an `<object>` element for each instance and in it a `<field>` for each field (`django/core/serializers/xml_serializer.py:Serializer`).

Its deserializer parses with `DefusedExpatParser`, which refuses a document type declaration, an entity declaration and an external reference (`django/core/serializers/xml_serializer.py:DefusedExpatParser`).
The XML deserializer raises `SuspiciousOperation` when a field's text holds an element with content of its own (`django/core/serializers/xml_serializer.py:check_element_type`).

The JSON and YAML deserializers parse the whole text, and the JSON Lines one a line at a time; each hands the Python objects to the Python deserializer, an iterator that makes a record into an object only when the iteration reaches it (`django/core/serializers/python.py:Deserializer._handle_object`):
Any other value goes through the target field's `to_python` and is not looked up (`django/core/serializers/base.py:deserialize_fk_value`).

Where the data has no primary key, the model has `natural_key` and its default manager `get_by_natural_key`, it first asks a provisional instance for its natural key and looks the row up; if the row is there, its key goes into the data, and a save then updates that row (`django/core/serializers/base.py:build_instance`).

`DeserializedObject.save` calls the base class's `Model.save_base` on `DeserializedObject.object` with `raw=True`, which, the comment says, bypasses any save the model defines (`django/core/serializers/base.py:DeserializedObject.save`).

A raw save writes the values the instance holds without asking its fields for their own, saves no parent, and passes `raw=True` to `pre_save` and `post_save` ([Saving an instance](../models/saving.md)), which tells a receiver, the documentation says, to leave other rows alone, as the database may not be consistent yet (`docs/ref/signals.txt`, [The signals Django sends](builtin-signals.md)).

`DeserializedObject.save_deferred_fields` is the second pass: it looks each deferred value up again, raising now if the object is still missing, sets it, and saves again (`django/core/serializers/base.py:DeserializedObject.save_deferred_fields`). loaddata saves every object first and makes this pass at the end ([Fixtures: dumpdata and loaddata](fixtures.md)); a foreign key deferred so must accept null for the first save (`docs/topics/serialization.txt`).
